title_en: Why EV fast charging slows down after 80 percent
title_fa: Why EV fast charging slows down after 80 percent
excerpt_en: EV fast charging will only take you so far - the speed slows down as you near a full charge. Turns out there's a good reason.
excerpt_fa: EV fast charging will only take you so far - the speed slows down as you near a full charge. Turns out there's a good reason.
content_en:
Why EV fast charging slows down after 80 percent
It doesn't mean you have a bad battery.
When the Tesla Model S launched in 2012, plugging it into a regular household outlet meant waiting more than 50 hours for a full charge, and all you got for that was up to 300 miles. The latest Model S is a different story: by the company's own figures, the car can add up to 200 miles in 15 minutes at a Supercharger. That's a very different car to live with.
But even now, charging doesn't stay fast. Look at how EV ads and spec sheets describe charging speed: "10 to 80 percent," "0 to 80 percent," almost never "to full." The first 80 percent is the fast part of the charge. Past it, the speed drops off, and the last stretch takes far longer than you'd expect. So what happens to the battery after 80 percent? It has nothing to do with bad EV charging habits, and everything to do with how the cell itself works.
What makes fast charging fast?
There are three ways to charge an EV: via a regular wall socket, a home or public charging station or a fast-charge station. All three do the same basic thing. They push electrons toward the battery, and inside its cells, lithium ions travel from one side (the cathode) and settle into the other (the anode). Then, as the car drives, those ions travel back into the cathode and supply the electric current. So "charging the battery" just means pushing the ions back into the anode.
The difference is how much power each one can push. A wall socket gives you a trickle of electricity, and a home or public charging station gives you several times more. A fast-charge station typically delivers 50kW to 350kW, and the newest ones go higher. So those ions get pushed much faster.
There's a second difference that makes a fast-charge station much more efficient. A wall socket or a charging post only supplies alternating current, so the car's own onboard charger has to turn it into direct current for the battery, and that little converter caps the speed. A fast-charge station does the conversion itself, in a big cabinet that doesn't have to fit inside a car, and sends direct current straight to the battery. The car just tells it how much it can take.
Why the last 20 percent is the slow part
Chargers push a constant current until the cell hits its voltage limit, then hold the voltage and let the current fall away. To see why that happens around 80 percent, picture the ions as passengers boarding an empty bus. They walk in one by one, find a seat and sit down. A faster charger just means more people come through the door each second. It doesn't add a single seat. Early on that works fine, because nearly every seat is free and everyone sits within a step or two of the door. Later the bus is mostly full. Each new passenger has to squeeze down the aisle, look for the last empty seat and wait for people ahead of them to shuffle along. Push more people through the door at that point and you just get a jam at the entrance.
A battery does the same thing. The anode is mostly graphite, and the lithium ions have to work their way into it, which is slow going. It takes even longer for the lithium to settle once the anode is nearly full. So past about 80 percent, the car asks the charger to cut the current, and the last stretch takes far longer than the first.
Why fast charging an EV to 100 percent doesn't work
Ions aren't people on a bus, though, and that's where pushing harder goes wrong. If the charger forces current into an anode that's already crowded, the lithium ions pile up at the surface faster than they can work their way in. With nowhere to go, they settle on the graphite as a thin layer of metallic lithium. That's called lithium plating. It's partially irreversible, so the battery permanently loses lithium it needs, and the metal can grow into spikes that eventually cause a short circuit. So the car slows the charge down on purpose, long before anything bad happens.
BYD recently announced a battery that it says can charge up to 97 percent in nine minutes. Its answer to the problem was to make the bus easier to get through, instead of shoving the passengers harder. The second-generation Blade Battery, unveiled in March 2026, rebuilds the graphite so its particles stand upright, which gives the ions a short, straight path instead of a winding one. BYD also changed the liquid the ions travel through so they move more easily, and the other side of the battery lets them leave faster. The result, according to BYD, is lower internal resistance and less heat, so the battery can take far more current. BYD says that, paired with its 1,500kW Flash Charger, the battery goes from 10 to 70 percent in five minutes and 10 to 97 percent in nine. The slowdown is still there. It just starts much later and ends much sooner. Carmakers do slow the charge on purpose, but they're only doing it because of the physics inside the cell.

title_en: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
title_fa: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
excerpt_en: Medium's new writing app embraces AI-assisted writing, despite growing controversy over the technology's role in publishing.
excerpt_fa: Medium's new writing app embraces AI-assisted writing, despite growing controversy over the technology's role in publishing.
content_en:
Online publishing platform Medium on Monday launched a new app, called TK, which aims to bring AI technology deeper into the writing process. The idea behind TK is to make it easier to turn ideas into written words by incorporating an AI assistant into the editor itself, allowing users to ask for help by typing “@TK” followed by their request or prompt.
In publishing and journalism, the term “TK” serves as a placeholder used to mark where missing information can be added later. The “TK” stands for “to come,” but uses a “K” instead of “C” as there are few English words where the “tk” letter combination exists, making it stand out more easily in written text where it could be caught by proofreaders.
In Medium’s app, TK takes on a new role as it tries to help users fill in the blanks.
The company suggests the AI assistant could help answer questions that you might normally have to switch to another tab to quickly look up, like how many days are in a particular month. The app could also pull in bits of writing you had previously saved to the app when you were still fleshing out your ideas.
In addition, Medium says TK will ship with particular skills for editorial feedback, headline feedback, and others that could match your draft to the style guide for Medium publications.
Medium’s move to embrace AI in the early stages of writing could prove controversial at a time when the publishing and literary worlds have been reckoning with the role that artificial intelligence has played in the creation of new long-form prose. Multiple authors have lost book deals over suspicions that they used AI technology to help them write, while other literary awards have come under scrutiny after winners were suspected of writing with AI assistance.
While writers have long used automated tools for proofreading and light grammatical edits, there is growing concern across the publishing industry that an AI assistant’s editorial “suggestions” can become the writing itself, instead of being reflective of the thoughts in the writer’s own mind.
But because AI models were trained on human writing, there are also questions around the reliability of AI detection tools in terms of their ability to properly determine when something was written with AI, rather than with its assistance, versus not at all.
TK leans into this debate, taking the side that these nuances will ultimately no longer matter in the end. Instead, the company celebrates what AI can bring to the world of writing, saying that “artificial intelligence makes writing more important, not less,” and proclaiming that “AI is a technology that has the power to amplify human intelligence and it uses the written word as a foundation.”
Still, Medium concedes that AI does raise the possibility of low-quality content and blurring the line between what’s human-written versus AI-written. To address these concerns, TK allows authors to publish notes that transparently explain how AI was used in their writing.
“This is a start of what we believe is required to publish in the AI era, which is to make the provenance of writing clear, transparent, and inspectable, right down to the prompting and source material,” Medium explained in a blog post about the launch.
In addition to writing assistance, TK will help users remember and organize what they had previously written and suggest writing prompts. The app can also optionally connect to your own AI agent through TK’s MCP server or Claude skill, so the app can better understand your projects, your positions, and other ideas that could be stored in your agent’s memory.
Meanwhile, the new app incorporates human feedback in a social layer, the company says, allowing writers to share their early drafts with others and get feedback.
At launch, TK is available on the web, but a desktop app is on the roadmap, Medium says. The app can import and export Markdown, but it’s not a Markdown app itself. The writing in TK is also not encrypted, as the app is designed for collaboration, but users will be able to set access control permissions on their work.
Medium, which is profitable, says TK will be a free tool for those with a Medium account.

title_en: Meta expands Instagram’s AI age-guessing tech globally
title_fa: Meta expands Instagram’s AI age-guessing tech globally
excerpt_en: Meta says it will use its AI technology to look for clues about people it suspects to be teenagers — even if they use an adult birthday.
excerpt_fa: Meta says it will use its AI technology to look for clues about people it suspects to be teenagers — even if they use an adult birthday.
content_en:
Meta announced on Monday that it’s expanding its AI-powered age-estimation technology on Instagram worldwide to identify more teens and place them under its Teen Account protections, as it faces numerous lawsuits accusing its platforms of harming teens.
The social media giant says it will use the AI technology to find people it suspects to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday.
Teen Accounts place users into a stricter account experience with additional safeguards, such as receiving direct messages only from people they follow or are already connected to, hiding harmful comments, and setting accounts to private by default.
Meta’s age-guessing tools use AI to analyze entire profiles for contextual clues, such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades. Meta also looks for these signals across different formats, such as posts, comments, bios, captions, and more. The company also looks at visual cues from photos and videos, including a person’s height or bone structure.
Meta said it’s continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook, with a similar global rollout planned for Threads later this year.
The global expansion comes as Meta reached settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every U.S. state and territory in August to resolve lawsuits alleging its platforms harm teens. As part of the settlements, Meta agreed to improve how it identifies teens and children under 13.
“We’ll continue to do our part to proactively ensure teens are in age-appropriate experiences on our apps,” Meta wrote in a blog post. “That’s why as part of our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia, we’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to children under 13. We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may belong to teens between the ages of 13 and 17 so we can ensure those accounts are placed in experiences designed for teens, even if they give us an adult birthday.”
Meta said parents in the U.S. will start seeing an in-feed video on Instagram explaining its approach to ensuring their teens are in age-appropriate protections.

title_en: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”
title_fa: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”
excerpt_en: Nvidia’s board is investigating Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld thinks it’s roughly a coin flip whether Huang stays on as CEO.
excerpt_fa: Nvidia’s board is investigating Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld thinks it’s roughly a coin flip whether Huang stays on as CEO.
content_en:
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “groundless smears and slanders,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised.
The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.
First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”
Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits, if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.
We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company
As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.
Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse.
So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea.”
Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips, the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”)
In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be...
content_fa:
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “groundless smears and slanders,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised.
The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.
First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”
Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits, if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.
We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company
As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.
Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse.
So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea.”
Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips, the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”)
In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be...

title_en: How to use your laptop as a second monitor
title_fa: How to use your laptop as a second monitor
excerpt_en: If you have an extra laptop lying around, you can connect it to your primary laptop with a wireless or wired connection for a free dual monitor set up.
excerpt_fa: If you have an extra laptop lying around, you can connect it to your primary laptop with a wireless or wired connection for a free dual monitor set up.
content_en:
How to use your laptop as a second monitor
Converting the device is not as easy as simply plugging in an HDMI cord, but here's what does work.
Whether you're gaming, working or simply browsing the web, adding a second monitor is one of the best ways to upgrade your workflow. Mirroring the display, which shows the same desktop on both screens, can be handy for presentations, while extending the display gives you one wider desktop. Extending the desktop into additional screen space means more visible tabs, easier multitasking and increased productivity. But making this change does not necessarily require buying a fancy setup. If you have a spare laptop lying around at home, you can make a few small tweaks to use dual monitors without going all-in on new hardware.
Converting your laptop into a second screen is fairly straightforward but not necessarily as simple as plugging in an HDMI cable. First you need to check your computer's compatibility, consider wired versus wireless options and tweak some settings on your system to smoothly extend or mirror the display. So how, exactly, do you turn your laptop into a second monitor? Here are the steps for Windows, Mac and Linux, as well as wired options via HDMI connections.
How to use a Windows laptop as a second monitor
If both your primary computer and the spare laptop you want to use as a second monitor are running Windows 10 or 11, extending or mirroring them is quite simple due to the operating systems' built-in wireless casting tools. These rely on Miracast, a functionality that enables connections between devices via Wi-Fi and requires only a quick workflow to set up.
To activate it, go to your spare laptop, open Settings, then System, then Projecting to this PC. Click Optional features, then View features, then select Wireless Display to add it. Once it installs, return to the same page and set it to Available everywhere, and open the Wireless Display app.
Now, you're ready to mirror or extend your display. On your main computer, press the Windows key + K, select the spare laptop from the list of available displays, enter the PIN and allow keyboard and mouse input. You can then choose to duplicate your screen or extend it, and you can switch anytime with Windows key + P. Keep in mind, this method of connecting your devices does require Wi-Fi on both machines, and you may experience some lag. Therefore, while it's great for presentations or organizing large numbers of tabs, it may not be the best choice for gaming.
Can I use other operating systems as a second monitor?
If both of your devices are Macs, you can use AirPlay to connect the two, but only if the MacBook is from 2018 or later. Once you've confirmed your device is compatible, go to the MacBook you want to use as the second screen, open System Settings, select General, then AirDrop & Continuity. Turn on AirPlay Receiver and then under Allow AirPlay for, select Current User. Make sure both MacBooks are signed into the same Apple ID to ensure a smooth connection. On your primary device, open System Settings, then Displays and click the plus sign from the dropdown menu to select your secondary device from the list. Decide if you want mirroring or extended display, which can be selected under settings. Like Windows' Miracast, Apple's AirPlay works over Wi-Fi and can thus have a slight delay. For a wired option with less lag, see the HDMI section below.
If connecting between two different operating systems, whether between a Windows PC and a MacBook or anything involving Linux, you will need software like Deskreen, a free, open-source tool that runs on Wi-Fi. To connect, make sure both computers are on the same Wi-Fi network, and download Deskreen on the main device. Deskreen will offer a QR code and URL. Open this on the spare laptop's browser to connect the devices. Deskreen mirrors the display by default. To extend to the spare laptop, you will need a cheap virtual display adaptor, or a "dummy plug," in your main computer's HDMI port. Like the other systems, any software that connects devices over Wi-Fi will have some lag, so consider the wired option below for gaming or other activities that rely on smoother connections.
Can I use an HDMI cable to connect my devices?
Most laptop HDMI ports are video-out only, so plugging two devices together with a cord will not directly allow you to extend or mirror displays. To work around this, get an HDMI-to-USB video capture card, which can be plugged into both laptops. Plug your main device's HDMI cable into the card, then plug the card's USB end into the spare laptop. The capture card will function as a webcam, so you can view the feed in your laptop's camera app or a free video app like OBS Studio, which runs on Windows, Mac and Linux.
If you are gaming and want to play a console without a TV, you can connect a PlayStation or a Nintendo Switch to the laptop in the same way. Again, there may be a small amount of lag but usually less than Wi-Fi-based connections, and it's unlikely to trip you up unless you are a competitive gamer. If none of these uses appeal to you, you can always use your old laptop to make a smart home hub.

title_en: Why your USB device isn't showing up on your MacBook and how you can fix it
title_fa: Why your USB device isn't showing up on your MacBook and how you can fix it
excerpt_en: If your USB device isn't showing up on your MacBook, the issue could be anything from a damaged cord to software troubles. Find out how to fix these problems.
excerpt_fa: If your USB device isn't showing up on your MacBook, the issue could be anything from a damaged cord to software troubles. Find out how to fix these problems.
content_en:
Why your USB device isn't showing up on your MacBook and how you can fix it
Fix hardware and software issues with some simple solutions.
USB wouldn't be what it is today without Apple. The format predates the original iconic iMac — but Apple's gumdrop-shaped computer helped popularize it by ditching all the legacy connectors that had been haunting the industry. USB became so commonplace, in fact, that the push came back to bite the company, with European Union regulations forcing it to ditch Lightning ports on iPhones. The days of Apple-exclusive ports are effectively over, MagSafe being the major remaining holdout.
Modern USB Mac accessories tend to be well-behaved. On occasion, though, macOS can fail to detect them, which is understandably maddening. With USB being as widespread as it is, anything less than a seamless experience feels unacceptable.
The good news is that there are known hardware and software explanations for why this happens, like damaged cords or an accessory that requires more power. In many situations the fixes are remarkably simple, particularly on the macOS side. There are rare instances, however, where you may need to seek outside help.
How to solve missing USB devices on your Mac
The first thing to remember is that by default, macOS requires you to give permission for accessories to connect. This prevents malware from being injected. At the same time, if you accidentally reject a permission prompt, a legitimate accessory won't transmit data until you give the green light. Charging should still work in either direction.
Typically, you can force macOS to re-display the permission prompt by unplugging an accessory and plugging it back in again. To minimize future hassle, though, go to Apple menu > System Settings > Privacy & Security, then scroll down to the Accessories section. Here you can choose Ask for new accessories, Automatically allow when unlocked or Always allow. It's best to skip that third option unless you're always around your Mac or in a very secure environment.
If that doesn't change anything, you might want to verify that macOS sees your device in the first place. Hold down the Option key, then click on Apple menu > System Information. If you see the accessory listed under Hardware, you may need to check the manufacturer's online support info. If it's invisible, or if it's detected but you keep getting an error message when plugging in, there may be more we can help with.
A probable cause in that regard is power. Some accessories may require more than a Mac's USB port can supply, in which case you should get a related message, and there may be a separate power cable you need to plug in. If there's no separate power on your accessory, however, the USB port itself may be the issue. Try alternate ports on your Mac or connecting directly if you were using a hub or dock as an intermediary. If you keep getting power-related warnings, you may want to talk to Apple tech support — it could be that your Mac just isn't feeding power to USB.
Other potential USB flaws and their fixes
Speaking of hubs and docks, don't forget that those often require their own power supplies. And even if they don't, things can go wrong with device chains, since of course they have to successfully transmit power or data across multiple hops. We recently had an experience with a Thunderbolt dock in which a wireless mouse receiver became unusable until it was plugged directly into a laptop — never mind that an SSD on the dock was doing just fine. It's always safer to skip the middleman if you have enough ports free.
Make sure that macOS is fully up-to-date by going to Apple menu > System Settings > General, then clicking on Software Update. Bugs or driver compatibility issues could hypothetically be interfering. Some accessories may also rely on proprietary software to do much of anything, in which case you'll want to make sure the latest version of that is installed. Check the Mac App Store or a manufacturer's website. External cards and drives need to use file system formats compatible with macOS, namely APFS, FAT or ExFAT.
Lastly, be sure that you're using the right type of USB cable for a device's power and bandwidth requirements and that there's no damage or debris interfering with either cables or ports. Things like lint and bent pins may be all it takes to block something from working. Lint, dust and grime can typically be cleaned out with an air can or by gently swiping a soft-tipped tool. As for damage, you'll likely just need to swap in a new cable, especially if there are any signs of browning or exposed wires. Those signal a fire hazard.

title_en: Which Canon Cameras Are Compatible With Its Free 3D Photo Software?
title_fa: Which Canon Cameras Are Compatible With Its Free 3D Photo Software?
excerpt_en: Canon cameras are often known for their versatility and compatibility with software programs. These cameras are best used with the free 3D photo software.
excerpt_fa: Canon cameras are often known for their versatility and compatibility with software programs. These cameras are best used with the free 3D photo software.
content_en:
Which Canon Cameras Are Compatible With Its Free 3D Photo Software?
Though not every camera is compatible there are a number on the market that are a perfect fit.
Canon wants to add a third dimension to your photos, and you won't need those pesky glasses to use it. At least, that's the goal of its Dual Pixel 3D imaging software. Released in October 2026, the free software's 3D converter app allows users to generate immersive 3D images and models without the use of specialized equipment.
Before you jump into 3D model rendering, you should know not every camera is compatible with Canon's software tool. This is because the system relies on your camera's Dual Pixel CMOS AF, a sensor-based autofocus found on select iterations of the company's EOS R series, which includes several of Engadget's highest-rated cameras of 2026.
Introduced by the camera maker in 2013, the sensor gives each pixel two photodiodes, which can either be combined to form a 2D image or read independently. Dual Pixel 3D runs these phase differences through a proprietary algorithm that converts your still image into a 3D rendering. Exportable in OBJ, GLB, and MP4 video formats, the images add hyper-realistic depth and texture to your photos.
As it stands, you can download the software for free from the company's website here. However, it is worth noting that the fine print of Canon's press release notes that while the 3D application "will initially be available free of charge," its "specifications and terms of use may change in the future." The caveat has caused some to speculate that the app may become a paid or subscription service.
Notably, the software is currently only compatible with the 2024 version or later of Windows 11. Once downloaded, extract the ZIP file and open the installer. After navigating through location, language, and licensing agreement windows, install the app and kick off your 3D journey. For a look at the Dual Pixel 3D Converter's instruction manual, visit Canon's website.
Compatible cameras and lenses
Before diving into how to use Canon's 3D imaging software, let's make sure you are using a compatible camera and lens. You can find a full list of cameras and lenses below or on Canon's website.
Canon's 3D imaging software requires a select group of EOS R cameras. The EOS R is Canon's most advanced series, featuring the company's lauded RF mount. With a 54mm diameter, the mount enables photographers to use more advanced lenses, decreasing the distance between the lens and senser. The mirrorless camera possesses a high FPS shutter, 12-pin communication system, cinematic 4k video at 120p, 8-stop image stabilization, and enhanced subject detection make the camera series Canon's most powerful — and expensive. The Canon EOS R5 Mark II, in particular, has garnered rave reviews from our writers.
There is, however, a catch. The earliest EOS R-series camera compatible with Canon's 3D modeling system is the EOS R5, which was released in 2020. Compatible cameras include:
- EOS R5 Mark II
- EOS R5
- EOS R6 Mark III
- EOS R6 Mark II
- EOS R7
- EOS R8 Mark II
- EOS R8
- EOS R10
You will also need to pair your EOS R-series camera with a compatible RF lens. The full list of compatible lenses include:
- RF24-70mm f/2.8 L IS USM
- RF24-50mm f/4.5-6.3 IS STM
- RF24-105mm f/4 L IS USM
- RF24-105mm f/4-7.1 IS STM
- RF35mm f/1.8 MACRO IS STM
- RF50mm f/1.8 STM
- RF70-200mm f/2.8 L IS USM
- RF70-200mm f/4 L IS USM
- RF85mm f/2 MACRO IS STM
- RF100mm f/2.8 L MACRO IS USM
- RF-S18-45mm f/4.5-6.3 IS STM
- RF-S18-150mm f/3.5-6.3 IS STM
Maximizing your 3D image
You can take several steps to maximize the quality of your 3D image. First, set your camera's aperture settings between f/5.6 and f/8. This keeps your subject in depth and reduces blurring and conversion errors. To boot, shoot at ISO 1600 or lower to minimize the noise in your photograph. Note that 3D models cannot be generated at ISO's greater than 3200. In your camera settings, you should also enable your Dual Pixel RAW or Add Distance to JPEGs settings, depending on whether you are taking RAW or JPEG images, respectively.
In terms of subject matter, the camera manufacturer suggests photographing objects with matte textures and thick, simple shapes. Examples include flowers with rounded petals, plants and leaves with little gloss, ceramic items, shallow plates, and food with rounded shapes. Moreover, avoid subjects with slender shapes, strong reflections, multiple blind spots, or significant blur.
When taking the photograph, center the subject and leave plenty of surrounding space. Shooting from a slightly elevated angle will help reduce blind spots and keep the subject at a distance 5 – 10x the focal length away. If the subject is dark, use the camera's flash or external lighting.
After you've taken your photo, import your image into the Dual Pixel 3D Converter software. Once booted up, you will find the thumbnail of your most recent photographs in the browser located on the lefthand side of the screen. From here, you can use the 3D Model Settings tab to customize your 3D generation process. Once generated, you can export your OBJ, GLB, or MP4 file to external 3D editing software. From there, the world is your 3D-oyster.

The mirrorless camera possesses a high FPS shutter, 12-pin communication system, cinematic 4k video at 120p, 8-stop image stabilization, and enhanced subject detection make the camera series Canon's most powerful — and expensive. The Canon EOS R5 Mark II, in particular, has garnered rave reviews from our writers.
There is, however, a catch. The earliest EOS R-series camera compatible with Canon's 3D modeling system is the EOS R5, which was released in 2020. Compatible cameras include:
- EOS R5 Mark II
- EOS R5
- EOS R6 Mark III
- EOS R6 Mark II
- EOS R7
- EOS R8 Mark II
- EOS R8
- EOS R10
You will also need to pair your EOS R-series camera with a compatible RF lens. The full list of compatible lenses include:
- RF24-70mm f/2.8 L IS USM
- RF24-50mm f/4.5-6.3 IS STM
- RF24-105mm f/4 L IS USM
- RF24-105mm f/4-7.1 IS STM
- RF35mm f/1.8 MACRO IS STM
- RF50mm f/1.8 STM
- RF70-200mm f/2.8 L IS USM
- RF70-200mm f/4 L IS USM
- RF85mm f/2 MACRO IS STM
- RF100mm f/2.8 L MACRO IS USM
- RF-S18-45mm f/4.5-6.3 IS STM
- RF-S18-150mm f/3.5-6.3 IS STM
Maximizing your 3D image
You can take several steps to maximize the quality of your 3D image. First, set your camera's aperture settings between f/5.6 and f/8. This keeps your subject in depth and reduces blurring and conversion errors. To boot, shoot at ISO 1600 or lower to minimize the noise in your photograph. Note that 3D models cannot be generated at ISO's greater than 3200. In your camera settings, you should also enable your Dual Pixel RAW or Add Distance to JPEGs settings, depending on whether you are taking RAW or JPEG images, respectively.
In terms of subject matter, the camera manufacturer suggests photographing objects with matte textures and thick, simple shapes. Examples include flowers with rounded petals, plants and leaves with little gloss, ceramic items, shallow plates, and food with rounded shapes. Moreover, avoid subjects with slender shapes, strong reflections, multiple blind spots, or significant blur.
When taking the photograph, center the subject and leave plenty of surrounding space. Shooting from a slightly elevated angle will help reduce blind spots and keep the subject at a distance 5 – 10x the focal length away. If the subject is dark, use the camera's flash or external lighting.
After you've taken your photo, import your image into the Dual Pixel 3D Converter software. Once booted up, you will find the thumbnail of your most recent photographs in the browser located on the lefthand side of the screen. From here, you can use the 3D Model Settings tab to customize your 3D generation process. Once generated, you can export your OBJ, GLB, or MP4 file to external 3D editing software. From there, the world is your 3D-oyster.

title_en: The disadvantages of buying tech from other countries
title_fa: The disadvantages of buying tech from other countries
excerpt_en: Importing a phone or a laptop can be appealing, especially if you can get a product you wouldn't otherwise have access to, but it has downsides.
excerpt_fa: Importing a phone or a laptop can be appealing, especially if you can get a product you wouldn't otherwise have access to, but it has downsides.
content_en:
The disadvantages of buying tech from other countries
Importing tech isn't too hard, but the downsides may not be worth it.
There are many reasons to import phones or other tech, whether you're buying it in person during a trip or via online marketplaces or importers. Your phone could die while you're travelling abroad, for example, forcing you to buy a replacement. Or maybe there's a perfect product for you, but it's not available where you live. Either way, buying tech from other countries is sometimes the only option.
Depending on the product, though, this can come with a catch or two. Buying devices from other regions can come with annoying restrictions. You might end up with slightly different hardware, lack warranty coverage or, in the worst case, not have access to core software or connectivity features. Here's what you should know before buying a new phone, laptop or any other tech product from overseas.
Not every device is built to work globally
A device can have different hardware configurations globally. In China, for example, certain iPhone models have slots for two physical SIMs. Conversely, US iPhones dropped the SIM tray starting with the iPhone 14, so you must use an eSIM instead. iPhones sold in China also get limited access to Apple Intelligence tools, even if you use it elsewhere.
Phones may pose issues with cellular bands. Manufacturers usually offer different versions of the same phone designed for specific bands in a given region. If you buy a phone in another country, it might not work on the US' 5G network, for example. This means you could lose access to carrier-specific features like VoLTE or Wi-Fi Calling if the device you're buying isn't certified for your network. It may seem minor, but it can be a headache if you plan to use it as your main device.
Other tech isn't free from potential issues, either. Laptops, for instance, can have different keyboard layouts depending on where you buy them. French laptops will use the AZERTY layout, and not every brand offers a QWERTY version in such markets. Depending on the product, power can be an issue too: imported products will likely use a different plug, so you'll need an adaptor, but that's not all. Watch out for voltages as well; the US uses 120V at 60Hz, but most of Europe and Asia use 220V to 240V, usually at 50Hz. Phone and laptop chargers usually work worldwide, but not all tech will.
Limited warranty and duties
Warranty is also an issue depending on what you're buying. Many manufacturers only provide tech support in the region where the device was sold. And if you're buying a product that isn't officially sold in the US, getting a broken part repaired can be tough, too. Some companies are more flexible when it comes to supporting devices purchased abroad, as is the case with AppleCare. Still, the company's warranty terms state that it may limit service for select devices, including the iPhone, to the country where the product was originally sold. Buying locally is still a safer bet if warranty is a priority.
If you're buying online, you also have to contend with import duties and shipping costs. The US has eliminated its $800 de minimis exemption for international parcels, so even small packages may get taxed quite heavily. International shipping isn't cheap, either. Most of the time, then, you have to really decide whether what you want to buy overseas is worth it.

title_en: 10 Apple products and features that transformed under Tim Cook's leadership
title_fa: 10 Apple products and features that transformed under Tim Cook's leadership
excerpt_en: Tim Cook led Apple for 15 years, during which time the company's offerings expanded and went through all kinds of changes.
excerpt_fa: Tim Cook led Apple for 15 years, during which time the company's offerings expanded and went through all kinds of changes.
content_en:
10 Apple products and features that transformed under Tim Cook's leadership
Apple changed a lot in the last 15 years.
When Tim Cook became Apple's CEO in 2011, he began leading what was already one of the world's most successful technology companies. The iPhone was driving Apple's growth, the iPad was still relatively new and the Mac was at the center of its computing business. Cook inherited an enormous ecosystem, then he spent 15 years finding new ways it could be put to use.
By the end of Cook's tenure, Apple had introduced entirely new product categories, moved the Mac to its own processors, turned the iPhone into a wallet and satellite communicator and built a services business worth more than $100 billion a year. Meanwhile, some of Apple's biggest changes weren't new products, but rather familiar ones that slowly evolved into something else.
There are now more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices, while the company brought in $416.2 billion in net sales in fiscal 2025. Apple's announcement on Cook's transition lays out the scale of the company he leaves behind. But the more interesting story is how under his leadership, Apple products took on entirely new forms and jobs.
1. The Apple Watch became much more than an iPhone accessory
When the Apple Watch launched in 2015, it was primarily an iPhone companion for notifications, communication, apps and activity tracking. Apple began expanding its health and fitness capabilities with Apple Watch Series 2, which added built-in GPS, swim tracking and more workout features.
The bigger shift came with Apple Watch Series 4 in 2018. With this, Apple added an ECG app and fall detection, giving the Watch capabilities that went beyond basics like tracking steps. The ECG could record a heart rhythm directly from the wrist, while fall detection could automatically contact emergency services if the wearer appeared to have taken a hard fall and remained immobile.
The watchOS 11 update in 2024 added sleep apnea notifications, the Vitals app and Training Load, giving you more ways to track and interpret health and fitness data. In 2025, the Apple Watch Series 11 introduced sleep scoring and hypertension notifications. While the watch started as an accessory for your iPhone, it now monitors a whole suite of metrics that the iPhone can't.
2. AirPods turned wireless earbuds into an Apple ecosystem
AirPods could have been just a pair of wireless earbuds for your iPhone, but Apple kept giving them more reasons to exist within the larger Apple ecosystem. Automatic pairing, seamless switching between devices, active noise cancellation and spatial audio made them an attractive option for all your music and other audio.
Apple has given AirPods an important role beyond entertainment, though. Starting with AirPods Pro 2, Apple added a scientifically validated Hearing Test, Hearing Aid functionality for people with mild to moderate hearing loss and Hearing Protection. These hearing health tools make support more accessible to lots of people. Meanwhile, the AirPods Pro 3 added heart rate sensing to track your workout effort with the buds you're likely already wearing while exercising.
Under Cook, Apple took a familiar product and expanded what it could do, without asking people to adopt an entirely new device.
3. Apple silicon gave the Mac a new foundation
For years, Apple built its own chips for the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch while relying on Intel processors for the Mac. That changed in 2020, when Apple announced a two-year transition to its own silicon. The move gave Mac computers a common architecture with Apple's other products, providing developers with a more unified platform for building software across the ecosystem.
The first Apple silicon Macs arrived later that year. Apple put the M1 chip in the MacBook Air, 13-inch MacBook Pro and Mac mini, combining the CPU, GPU, Neural Engine and other components into a single system-on-a-chip. This helped Apple push the Mac toward the same performance and power efficiency that had come to define its mobile devices.
The difference between Apple's processors and Intel's isn't just speed. After Apple took over this core piece of Mac hardware, it had holistic control of the hardware design, chips inside and macOS itself. This helped the Mac overcome its midlife crisis.
4. The iPhone camera became a serious photography tool
What started as a convenient way to snap a picture became a sophisticated camera system with multiple lenses, computational photography, Night mode and some serious video capabilities.
The iPhone 11 was a big turning point. It featured an Ultra Wide camera, Night mode and Deep Fusion, which uses machine learning to process photos pixel by pixel for more detail and less noise. The iPhone 12 Pro then added Apple ProRAW, combining Apple's computational photography with the flexibility of a RAW file for those who wanted more control over their images.
Apple's more recent iPhones have continued this progress. The iPhone 15 Pro brought a 48MP main camera, multiple focal-length options, 48MP ProRAW and professional video features including ProRes recording to external storage. Our iPhone 15 review highlighted the camera as a major part of the upgrade. Later, our iPhone 17 review covered more camera improvements, including a new Center Stage front camera and upgraded rear cameras. For many people, their iPhone camera is the way they take pictures, and what all other smartphone cameras are judged against.
5. Apple Pay turned the iPhone into a wallet
Apple Pay is easy to take for granted because it feels so normal now. But in 2014, putting a payment system directly into the iPhone people already carried everywhere gave the device a new role: replacing the cards in their wallet. Apple Pay eventually expanded beyond in-store purchases to apps, websites and other Apple devices like the Apple Watch.
10 years after its launch, the company stated that Apple Pay was used by hundreds of millions of people across 78...

title_en: Those white cameras mounted above traffic lights serve a little-known purpose
title_fa: Those white cameras mounted above traffic lights serve a little-known purpose
excerpt_en: Many people are up in arms over Flock and similar cameras that can track you when you drive. But these cameras are there for a whole different reason.
excerpt_fa: Many people are up in arms over Flock and similar cameras that can track you when you drive. But these cameras are there for a whole different reason.
content_en:
Those white cameras mounted above traffic lights serve a little-known purpose
Unlike Flock cameras, they're only meant to keep traffic flowing.
Automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) are nothing new, but reported abuses have made drivers understandably wary of the cameras made by Flock and other companies, to the point of wanting to find out where they are so they can be avoided. While that added attention has made intersection cameras seem more visible than ever, not every camera you see mounted above the road serves the same purpose. Most cameras on roadways aren't used to track individual drivers, but rather to monitor traffic conditions.
Aside from ALPRs, cameras meant to track people running red lights are also controversial. They're banned in many states, and they're rare even where they're allowed. Far more common are cameras used to monitor traffic conditions in real time or automatically control traffic lights.
Most cameras are there to control the flow of traffic
Distinct from cameras used to catch drivers speeding or running red lights, traffic cameras aren't designed to capture evidence for law enforcement. Instead, they're meant to be watched live to monitor the current state of traffic and keep an eye out for accidents. This real-time data can be used by local transportation departments to help keep traffic moving, by overriding automatic light timings in some cases, or to alert first responders when needed. These systems can also be used to track traffic patterns over time, helping traffic engineers determine when changes need to be made to roadways or signals to control congestion.
In many cases, the cameras mounted on traffic lights are tied to automatic signaling systems rather than providing a live video feed. These cameras send data to control systems that determine when lights should cycle. Engineers can designate a section of the video frame that the camera should monitor for the presence of cars. When a car enters that space, it triggers the light to change based on a timing sequence that pre-programmed for each individual roadway. In addition to video cameras, these systems often use radar, infrared cameras and electromagnetic detectors built into roads to detect the presence of vehicles.
Exactly what the cameras on roadways are used for varies widely based on where they are. Local laws determine which types of cameras are allowed to be installed in the first place, and how they're used depends on the needs of a particular intersection. While there's plenty of justified concern over the prevalence of Flock cameras and other ALPRs, chances are when you see a camera mounted above a traffic light, it's just there to keep things moving.

title_en: SpaceXAI Grok Bot availability just keeps growing - here's which plans offer it
title_fa: SpaceXAI Grok Bot availability just keeps growing - here's which plans offer it
excerpt_en: SpaceXAI 's Grok Bot can handle multi-step work on a cloud computer, but you'll need to figure out the jumble of subscription plans first.
excerpt_fa: SpaceXAI 's Grok Bot can handle multi-step work on a cloud computer, but you'll need to figure out the jumble of subscription plans first.
content_en:
SpaceXAI Grok Bot availability just keeps growing - here's which plans offer it
Peruse an eye-popping array of subscriptions for a product still finding its feet.
SpaceXAI's Grok Bot is already much easier to access than it was on day one. The company expanded its agent to SuperGrok, Cursor Pro and all Cursor Teams plans, adding Grok Bot to cheaper tiers while keeping it on the more expensive ones. X Premium+ subscribers can also link their accounts for access. (More on all this in a moment.) Bottom line: There is a growing pile of subscriptions plans for this relatively new product, so we'll help you get your bearings.
Grok Bot is designed to work inside other software on your behalf, and SpaceXAI says its Bots are "AI teammates" that can "finish jobs end to end, and only come back when something needs your approval." Remove the marketing spin and the concept is pretty simple: provide it with a task, let it handle the tedious clicks and return when it requires assistance. That sounds spiffy, but what actually makes it tick?
What can Grok Bot actually do?
Each SpaceXAI Bot works on a persistent computer in Cursor's cloud and has access to a browser, a file system and a terminal. You give it an outcome and access to the tools it needs, then the job can keep running even after your own computer is closed.
In practice, you could have a Bot research sales prospects, look at a CRM for existing activity, compose personalized outreach and leave it for your approval. SpaceXAI also suggests using it to reproduce software bugs, generate customer-health reports and create executive digests from email, calendars and other related sources.
Bots can carry over context from one conversation to another and can repeat workflows at a scheduled time. That's where Grok Bot becomes less of a conversational bot and more of a bot that you delegate to do work for you.
It still has its limits though. Websites can block automation or throw up a CAPTCHA, login request or other step that only humans can complete. Potentially consequential actions can be queued for approval before the Bot proceeds. Early users have also reported that some workflows still require more babysitting than the "go away and do it" promise implies. It's still in beta, after all.
Which plans include Grok Bot?
Cursor Pro costs $20 per month, Pro+ costs $60 and Ultra costs $200. Teams Standard is $40 per user per month and Teams Premium is $120. All members of a self-serve Cursor Teams plan are granted access to Grok Bot, and Enterprise customers can request access from their account team.
On the Grok side, SuperGrok is $30 per month, SuperGrok Plus is $100 per month and SuperGrok Heavy is also eligible. X Premium+ subscribers can also connect their accounts, with the plan costing $40 a month in the United States. Enterprise access is handled separately, with Grok and Cursor Enterprise customers now able to use Grok Bot through their organizations. There is also a usage-based Grok Bot free trial with a seven-day window.
Paid access isn't unlimited. Included Grok Bot usage resets weekly, and extra usage can continue through the account's shared on-demand spending (if enabled). Cursor doesn't specify a set number of Bot jobs for the free trial, saying the credit is measured by agent steps and tokens rather than message count.
This seemingly disorganized list of subscriptions makes sense in light of the business moves involved in the initiative. In April 2026, Cursor partnered with SpaceX to speed up model training on SpaceXAI's Colossus infrastructure. In August 2026, SpaceX acquired Cursor. and Grok Bot was officially introduced that same month.

In August 2026, SpaceX acquired Cursor. and Grok Bot was officially introduced that same month.

title_en: Should you make the switch to Google Pixel from Samsung Galaxy?
title_fa: Should you make the switch to Google Pixel from Samsung Galaxy?
excerpt_en: While Samsung Galaxy phones deliver flagship power, Google Pixel phones have lots of benefits, including faster updates and minimal bloatware.
excerpt_fa: While Samsung Galaxy phones deliver flagship power, Google Pixel phones have lots of benefits, including faster updates and minimal bloatware.
content_en:
Should you make the switch to Google Pixel from Samsung Galaxy?
It depends what you're after: minimal bloatware or flagship power.
Google revealed the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro in August 2026, flagships with new AI features and camera improvements that helped them go toe-to-toe with the Samsung Galaxy S26 lineup. While they may never hit Samsung's sales numbers, the Pixel line has often led the Android pack on the features front, and this year is no different. Samsung might deliver flagship power, but some users will find greater utility with the Pixel 11's camera upgrades including the new Camera Looks filters and built-in scrolling teleprompter.
There's more to a smartphone than a spec sheet, and if you want the latest Android features first, a Google Pixel phone is the way to go. Samsung's One UI updates are fairly frequent but still play second fiddle to Google's phones. Other factors like performance and camera prowess demand a more nuanced comparison. If you're considering switching to a Pixel from Samsung territory, here's what you need to know.
What is so special about the Google Pixel?
Pixels lead the industry when it comes to packing minimal bloatware and essential features. While they may not have stock Android, there's no Bixby assistant to disable or duplicate Samsung apps to uninstall here. Seven years of Android updates and quarterly Pixel Drops beat similar offerings from other manufacturers since Google's phones get them first. Look past high-end phones, and you'll notice that Samsung's Galaxy A phones only have six years of OS updates compared to the Pixel A-series' seven years.
While earlier Pixel phones leaned on software tricks against Samsung's industry-leading hardware, that gap is shrinking. The Pixel 11 Pro XL has cameras that rival those on the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. Quicker shots, near-zero shutter lag and natural color processing compared to Samsung's vivid colors mean that some say Google's phones are better at everyday photography. However, the Galaxy S26 Ultra beats the Pixel 11 Pro XL in battery life, with quicker charging and better endurance.
If you've already invested in one of the ecosystems with a device like the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9, optimal compatibility is another factor to consider. The Samsung Health Monitor app, for instance, is exclusive to Samsung devices and lets the Galaxy Watch 9 monitor blood pressure levels and ECG signals.
Should you switch from a Galaxy to a Pixel?
Despite these strengths, a new Google Pixel is only worth considering if you have an old Galaxy phone that you want to upgrade. Newer phones like the Samsung Galaxy S26 compete favorably with Google's best. The Pixel 11 Fold's form factor isn't quite as exciting as the passport-style Galaxy Z Fold 8. And if you're in the market for a Galaxy Z Flip or a phone with stylus support, there's no Google equivalent.
While the Pixel 11 lineup's Tensor G6 processor is efficient at day-to-day tasks, it suffers in high-demand games and raw benchmarks compared to the S26's speedy Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. This processor also lets the Galaxy S26 Ultra capture video at up to 8K at 30 fps and 4K at 120 fps compared to the Pixel 11 Pro's 4K at 60 fps. The latter can only process videos in 8K by using a Video Boost feature that relies on cloud computing.
Pixel owners also miss out on DeX, Samsung's desktop experience that runs circles around Android's fledgling desktop mode. Samsung has also been building One UI's customization options, with features like Modes and Routines that let users set up "If This Then That" routines for driving, bedtime or simple home automation. Google's AI features are no slouch though, from Gemini taking over tasks like phone calls or hailing an Uber to the Magic Capture feature that shoots videos and picks the best pictures from them.
Picking between the two depends on your priorities. While power users will find Samsung's approach more appealing, the Pixels are great everyday phones with faster updates.

title_en: What is the Slate Telematics Module and what can it be used for?
title_fa: What is the Slate Telematics Module and what can it be used for?
excerpt_en: When you buy a Slate Truck, you only pay for the tech you want, and that includes connectivity between the vehicle and your phone. Is this a minimalist's dream?
excerpt_fa: When you buy a Slate Truck, you only pay for the tech you want, and that includes connectivity between the vehicle and your phone. Is this a minimalist's dream?
content_en:
What is the Slate Telematics Module and what can it be used for?
Want remote access in the Slate Truck? You'll need its $275 accessory and, eventually, a service subscription.
When you buy a Slate Truck, you only pay for the tech you want, and Slate is taking that idea pretty far. There's no built-in infotainment system on its $24,950 Blank Slate, and even the hardware that enables the truck to communicate via a cellular network is optional. Slate offers that connection as a separate $275 Telematics Module.
Slate describes it as a "plug-and-play solution...enabling features like remote access and battery pre-conditioning." It's compatible with all Slate body styles, and the price includes the module and a one-year service subscription.
You don't need the module for driving the truck. Slate says its upcoming free app isn't mandatory either. The Telematics Module is just another choice in a truck design that is a minimalist's delight, allowing users to opt in or out of equipment that many newer vehicles include by default.
What the Slate Telematics Module actually does
It's important to understand the difference between Slate's app and its Telematics Module. Slate told SAE Media that the base truck has no modem. The app will show charge status and battery health, help drivers find charging stations, and support service-related functions. The module adds a cellular path between the phone and truck, which is what makes remote access possible.
The most practical confirmed use might be battery pre-conditioning. An EV battery performs differently in cold weather, and pre-conditioning can warm the battery before driving. The ability to do that remotely may be important for someone who leaves their Slate outside during the winter months (especially if the truck is plugged in).
The term "remote access" is less clear. Slate hasn't specified whether that phrase covers remote locking and unlocking, vehicle location, cabin climate controls or detailed diagnostics. The company also hasn't explained how its battery pre-conditioning feature works or if remote access includes cabin heating and cooling.
The module's hardware can be installed by the owner. Slate rates the job as intermediate, states that standard tools will suffice, and estimates that installation should take between 30 minutes and two hours.
Who is the Telematics Module for?
The Telematics Module makes the most sense for owners who want to access their Slate remotely. If you're drawn to this minimalist truck, in part, because it lacks connected-car hardware, the added cost of a modem might not be appealing.
There's another cost to keep an eye on. The $275 purchase price covers only the first year of service, and Slate has not said what connectivity will cost after the first year or what features will cease to work if the owner doesn't renew.
This setup is unusual compared with mainstream connected vehicles. Ford mentions a 5G modem in the 2026 Maverick and states that once the modem is activated, it will unlock free app features such as remote lock and unlock, remote start and vehicle information. Rivian includes mobile app remote commands such as lock and unlock as standard, but charges separately for more advanced connected features.
Connectivity also raises a privacy question. Slate told SAE Media that it has no plans to sell driver data. The optional module will enable the truck to exchange information, though Slate hasn't specified what data the module will send or store.
The Blank Slate costs $24,950 plus a $1,450 destination fee, and pre-orders are currently limited to U.S. residents.

title_fa: Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
excerpt_en: On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees...
excerpt_fa: On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees...
content_en:
On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below.
Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
In the memo Nvidia’s CEO acknowledges having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
In the memo Nvidia’s CEO acknowledges having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
To my colleagues at NVIDIA,
I owe my family and all of you an apology.
I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.
Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.
To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.
To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.
Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.
My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.
— Jensen

title_en: Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
title_fa: Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
excerpt_en: Soul Glo has a new record called NA I'M GON GRAB ALLAT coming out in January, and I, for one, can not wait. While two singles have dropped, it's not enough to truly tide me over, so I've been revisiting Songs to Yeet at the Sun and my favorite album of 2022 - Diaspora Problems....
excerpt_fa: Soul Glo has a new record called NA I'M GON GRAB ALLAT coming out in January, and I, for one, can not wait. While two singles have dropped, it's not enough to truly tide me over, so I've been revisiting Songs to Yeet at the Sun and my favorite album of 2022 - Diaspora Problems....
content_en:
Soul Glo has a new record called NA I’M GON GRAB ALLAT coming out in January, and I, for one, can not wait. While two singles have dropped, it’s not enough to truly tide me over, so I’ve been revisiting Songs to Yeet at the Sun and my favorite album of 2022 — Diaspora Problems.
Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
Diaspora Problems is one of the 21st century’s best punk albums.
Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
Diaspora Problems is one of the 21st century’s best punk albums.
“Gold Chain Punk (whogonbeatmyass?)” is an opening salvo for the ages. Bong rip, into a catchy-as-hell hardcore riff, with frontman Pierce Jordan ranting. Then comes the half-time stomp as Jordan gets fully unhinged, screaming “Who gon beat my ass? Who the fuck gon beat my ass?” From here on out, as the music shifts through a few different sections, the energy never comes down. Jordan shreds his vocal cords, begging, “Can I live?” Before finally spelling it out for anyone still confused:
Say more, say less, it’s all the same
When it’s time to die we can meet outside
To see who gon feel my pain
The record barely lets up from here on out. “Coming Correct” opens with a cough and a steady 808, giving you literally three seconds to catch your breath before Jordan jumps on the mic shouting, “I try to listen the way, I wanna be listened to.” The song starts stacking elements quickly, reaching full firestorm by 25 seconds in, and then doesn’t let up for the rest of its three-minute runtime.
The front chunk of the record is just perfect unrelenting hardcore song after perfect unrelenting hardcore song. Jordan’s crazed charisma is undeniable as he ricochets between leftist rhetoric, goofy bits about smoking weed, and vulnerable explorations of his struggles with depression. You’d be forgiven for struggling to keep up with his rapid-fire delivery, which owes almost as much to modern rappers as it does to classic hardcore acts like Minor Threat or Bad Brains.
Track six, “Driponomics,” fully embraces those more modern influences with trap snares, wall-rattling 808 kicks, and a guest verse from Mother Maryrose. The sampled guitar calls to mind the sax squeals favored by the Bomb Squad… just heavier.
The album eventually culminates in “Spiritual Level Of Gang Shit,” which features guest verses from McKinley Dixon and Lojii over gently echoed guitar melodies and dub-inspired groove. Then, around the 2:20 mark, things take a turn as the guitars turn punishing and the drums shift to a standard hardcore beat. But the song hasn’t reached its final form yet. That comes almost a minute later when the horn section kicks in.
Next to other modern hardcore standard bearers like Turnstile, Soul Glo might almost seem like traditionalists heavily influenced by the DC scene. But Diaspora Problems shows their ambition and willingness to take risks. Soul Glo plays with genre, is confrontational in its politics, and is generally just uncompromising.
Oh, and they put on a hell of a live show (I’ve seen them at least four times now). Don’t miss their incredible Tiny Desk Concert either, which I’m pretty sure is the first mosh pit to even open up in the NPR offices.
Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Qobuz, Deezer, YouTube Music, Apple Music, and Spotify.
